title: False Choice
plain_title: A review of the fiscal 2027 preliminary budget and its gap
what_they_audited: A Citizens Budget Commission report analyzing New York City's fiscal year 2027 preliminary budget.
background: The preliminary budget raised the revenue forecast by $7.6 billion over fiscal years 2026 and 2027 while adding $12.3 billion to the spending forecast.

findings.plain: City spending has grown much faster than inflation over the past decade.
findings.quote: Fiscal year 2026 spending is $16 billion higher than if it had grown at the rate of inflation since fiscal year 2017.

findings.plain: Between fiscal years 2021 and 2025, city-funded spending grew faster than the tax revenue supporting it.
findings.quote: City funded spending (adjusted for prepayments) grew 6.8 percent annually, outpacing the 5.2 percent annual growth in tax revenues

findings.plain: Across four fiscal years the city's obligations are on track to exceed the revenue it collects.
findings.quote: The City is on track to spend $5.8 billion more than it took in over four years.

findings.plain: After adjusting for the updated revenue and spending forecasts, the two-year budget gap is $9.4 billion.
findings.quote: The combined fiscal year 2026 and 2027 budget gap totals $9.4 billion

findings.plain: The budget draws on the rainy day fund and the Retiree Health Benefits Trust, which the report describes as one-time resources.
findings.quote: The proposed drawdown from the Revenue Stabilization Fund (“rainy day fund”) and Retiree Health Benefits Trust (RHBT) are one-shots...

findings.plain: The savings in the plan amount to a small share of annual spending.
findings.quote: The proposed savings are too small, just 2 percent of annual spending.

numbers.label: Fiscal 2026 spending above an inflation-only path
Four-year shortfall of revenue against obligations

Added to the spending forecast in the budget

recommendations: Reject the tax increases under consideration.
Reduce ineffective spending and improve operational efficiency, including in education, procurement and administrative operations.
Right-size spending where demand has changed, such as adjusting school funding for declining enrollment and managing growth in the FHEPS housing voucher program.

Build and maintain reserves by leaving the rainy day fund and the Retiree Health Benefits Trust untouched, including $1 billion of in-year reserves, and by requiring deposits to the Revenue Stabilization Fund when the economy is growing while limiting withdrawals to a recession or severe emergency.
